articleTitle: Transient effects in application of PWM inverters to induction motors
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Standard squirrel cage induction motors are subjected to nonsinusoidal wave shapes, when supplied from adjustable frequency inverters. In addition to causing increased heating, these wave patterns can be destructive to the insulation. Pulse width modulated (PWM) inverter output amplitudes and risetimes are investigated, and motor insulation capabilities are discussed. Voltage reflections are simulated for various cable lengths and risetimes and are presented graphically. Simulations confirm potential problems with long cables and short risetimes. Application precautions are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Measuring the noise level of loaded electric motors
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Methods for measuring the noise level of loaded motors on the manufacturer's test floor have been evaluated. Methods considered include quieting the loading device, utilizing a nose testing enclosure at the load test area, and utilizing the sound intensity measuring technique. Each method is examined, and the merits of each are reviewed. It is concluded that testing the noise level of loaded electric motors is feasible by any of the three methods examined. The choice of test method is dictated primarily by the nature of prevailing conditions in the manufacturer's shop, along with considerations of economics and convenience of usage. In the case history outlined, these factors point toward the use of the sound intensity method. The test results and evaluations made using the sound intensity approach show that very good accuracy is achievable and that the method lends itself to application in a shop environment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A different approach to a paper machine retrofit
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Digital control of drive equipment has provided unique opportunities to utilize silicon-controlled rectifier DC-drive systems. It is shown that an economical, functional, and reliable system can be obtained by selecting new modern digital components and logic controls to upgrade an operating drive section. The authors describe the selection process, changes that took place in the design of a system, retrofitting of the new equipment to reusable machine drives, and the installation. The machine start-up and the operation of the equipment after the changeover have provided verification that combining existing DC section electric drives with new digital controllers can be an economic alternative.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Justification for AC vs. DC drive systems
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is pointed out that AC variable-speed drives are seeing more widespread use in the pulp and paper industry. This is due to the reliability and low cost of the AC induction motor, combined with the recently improved economy and performance of AC drives. It is noted that, even though the up-front cost of an AC drive control, is greater than that of the DC drive, there are many factors to consider that can quickly make up the difference. Conservative data are presented which indicate a 17% savings as a percentage of total system and installation cost using AC drives. Some end users have experienced up to 30% savings.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rating considerations for squirrel cage induction motors operated with variable frequency drives
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author addresses rating considerations for squirrel cage induction motors operated with variable-frequency drives. The motors addressed are assumed to be larger than 20 HP and of three-phase design. It is shown that for the majority of applications, consisting of centrifugal fans or pumps, standard motors with 1.15 to 1.2 service factors can be rerated for inverter use with 1.0 service factors. For more rigorous applications, such as constant torque, constant horsepower, or reciprocating loads, the selection of motors more suited for inverters has been gaining popularity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design considerations in high power adjustable frequency drives
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The design of variable-frequency drives above 250 HP is considered. The author elaborates on various problems associated with the power circuit, the auxiliary power supply, and the controller design specific to high-power variable-frequency drives. The discussion is based on the PWM (pulse width modulation) type of drive, as this is presently the most popular choice. Solutions are proposed, and an effort is made to predict future trends.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Protection philosophy and relay selection for large AC motors
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Issues related to protection and relay selection for large AC motors are examined. A few of the problems which must be solved by motor application and relaying engineers are discussed. Particular attention is given to relay redundancy requirements, current transformers, relay data availability, and protective features.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The ultra efficient amorphous substation transformer
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author describes amorphous core transformer technology development and broadly compares the technical characteristics and performance to those of conventional high-efficiency silicon steel transformers. How amorphous transformer technology can reduce industrial power losses and improve productivity is addressed. It is pointed out that the ultraefficient amorphous metal core transformer technology offers the industry a conservation alternative which can help the energy equation and boost productivity. Amorphous core distribution transformers (10 kVA through 2500 kVA) have become a technological and commercial reality with potential for reducing US utility losses and stretching scarce generating capacity by over 7000 MW, equivalent to 60 billion kWh annually. Application of this advanced technology to liquid filled industrial substation transformers (10 kVA through 2500 kVA) will provide potential for additional conservation of over 2500 MW, equivalent to 22 billion kWh annually.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: IEEE 1202 flame testing of cables for use in cable tray
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The new IEEE 1202, IEEE Standard for Flame Testing of Cables for Use in Cable Tray in Industrial and Commercial Occupancies, is described. This flame test standard will: (1) contribute to harmonization of Canadian and US standards, most likely becoming a North American standard and eventually replacing the current UL and CSA tray cable flame tests; (2) provide more flame retardant cables for use in cable trays; and (3) address the valid criticism that not all constructions in a product line will pass the existing flame tests since only a 7/C or a 9/C 12 AWG (3.31-mm/sup 2/) construction is tested (under this new standard, there is a very high probability that all constructions will pass the flame test). Adoption of this standard may eliminate some present cable constructions from use in cable trays or at least require some redesign to comply with the flame test.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Synchronous motor field controllers and their application
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The effects of field voltage, field current, power factor, and VAr controllers on a paper mill power system are discussed. The author reviews synchronous motor response to load and field current changes with respect to power factor and VAr flow. He examines what happens to the power system during load swings. with the various field controllers applied. It is shown that the VAr controller is the controller of choice for constantly changing loads. A method is advanced to help control the total mill VAr flow using VAr controllers and communications equipment currently available.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design considerations of a serial communications system for adjustable frequency drives
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author describes the design of a simple and effective serial communications system for adjustable frequency drives. It is designed to provide the attributes of simplicity, flexibility, and room for future expansion. A network of three AC adjustable frequency drives has been set up and tested with a menu-driven user-friendly program which has been developed to run under the MS-DOS environment. Based on the results from the tests performed on the terminal and network software, the communications system designed for the AC drives has proven to be successful with respect to both man-machine and machine-machine interfaces.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Future trends in total digital control of variable speed drives for industrial applications
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The essential rudiments of digital control hardware and software as well as the potential extension of this technology to a dedicated CAD/CAE (computer-aided design/engineering) environment for design of motor drive systems are discussed. These systems, which are intensely application-dependent, have been traditionally designed and manufactured using combinations of logic controllers, computers, power circuits, and analog control boards connected together to achieve the final goal. The proposed CAD environment strives to consolidate the drive systems design requirements in such a way as to allow implementation of these designs within a framework of a standard library of hardware and software. The end result is a production environment where all designs are optimally manufacturable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Short circuit protection of low voltage motor branch circuits, by HRC II-C fuses
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is pointed out that HRCII-C fuses meeting CSA Specification C22.2 no.106-M 1985 and complying with the requirements for type gG fuses of IEC269-1986 provide proven backup protection to IEC rated contactors and motor starters, ensuring Type 2 coordination and enabling their motor starting capabilities to be fully utilized. HRCII-C fuses provide lower power losses than the HRCI-J fuses for the same application, which is a significant factor in modern compact motor control centers. It is further noted that the pending revision of C22.2 no.106 will rectify a weakness in the 1985 edition by recognizing the fact that the HRCII-C fuses can meet let through limits significantly less than those indicated in that edition.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Correcting mill power factor with a synchronous condenser
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author compares the use of capacitors and synchronous condensers and their impact on a plant's power factor. He discusses condenser start-up and operation, and its power factor monitoring and correction circuitry. He also examines condenser sizing, and shows typical payback justification.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parallel operation of Darlington transistors in a large 480 V, 700 HP induction motor drive
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Bipolar transistors have been used successfully in variable-frequency induction motor drive equipment. A practical approach to paralleling bipolar Darlington 600 A transistor modules in order to produce 700 HP, 480 V equipment, is described. Emphasis is placed on the base drive circuitry, the methods of controlling parasitic inductance in the power circuit, and the mechanical arrangement of the equipment. Darlington transistors could be applied straightforwardly in parallel conjunctions as long as simple precautions were followed. The resulting equipment contained liberal safety margins in current and in operating temperature. This provided conditions conducive to long life and reliability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Nuggets of Knowledge revisited (power distribution)
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: In the paper 'Nuggets of Knowledge', presented at the May, 1976, IEEE Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference, W.C. Bloomquist and E. J. Kayfes presented an array of power distribution topics selected through a poll of various committees. In the present work, the author provides further background on some of the topics, updates others, and introduces some new ones. The following topics are covered: (1) MVA fault calculation method; (2) rule-of-thumb for motor starting voltage drop; (3) rule-of-thumb for voltage change due to switching capacitors; (4) need for regulator to control VArs in a utility tie; (5) rule-of-thumb for amount of capacitance to connect to an induction motor; (6) Is a higher system voltage economical for mills?; (7) 'new' rules in selecting voltage ratings of power cables; (8) bifurcation; (9) low resistance grounding of a delta connected power system; (10) selection of synchronous chipper transformers based on impact loading considerations; and, (11) transformer protection update.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Requirements, specification and design considerations for implementation of a PLC-based burner management system
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: A knowledge base of burner management systems (BMSs) as adapted to a programmable controller platform is described. Emphasis is placed on the safety and reliability aspects of the system, including both the hardware components and the software components that interact with the hardware. It is concluded that safety and reliability are the keys to the successful implementation of a burner management system. The subsystems must be designed with an awareness of these two elements and combined to form an integrated system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Condensing generation-Is it economic?
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The addition of a condensing turbine offers desirable flexibility in the operation of a pulp and paper mill electric generating plant. However, condensing may be a costly alternative. The authors investigate the economics of condensing turbines and outline a method for assessing cost versus benefits. The use of incremental values is essential to the evaluation. Case studies are provided involving operating the condenser for continuous generation and condensing operation for electric load peak shaving. It is pointed out that, when making an economic evaluation of a condenser, the following are the principal considerations: fuel costs; equipment costs; value of electricity displaced by generation; annual operating hours; discount rate; and project life.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Using new technology to improved reliability of an industrial cable distribution system
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The service history of medium-voltage power cables on the US plant sites of a major industrial manufacturer from 1961 through 1990 is summarized. In past years this company tended to be reactive, using specifications, diagnostic testing, and maintenance practices to manage the reliability of their cable distribution systems. Several new technologies in insulation systems, terminations, splices, and installation techniques, introduced in recent years, have allowed a more proactive stance to be taken. In addition, because of some specific failure problems, a highly qualified in-house team has been formed to evaluate existing and future technologies and new insulation materials to assure a reliable cable system. It is concluded that the combination of materials and engineering technology has brought a new dimension to the process of installing and maintaining reliable cable systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Implementation of a maintenance apprenticeship training program
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: In February 1987, the maintenance department at Bowater Carolina Division began a new maintenance apprenticeship program. Several factors in the development of this program are discussed. First, the need for the program had to be established. Second, an agreement had to be reached on a framework for the program. Then, the means of starting and administering the program could be discussed. The program's successes and future potential are brought out. Appendices giving details of the program are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Installation and start-up of a PLC based burner management system
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is pointed out that in recent years, the Black Liquor Recovery Boiler Advisory Committee (BLRBAC) and Factory Mutual (FM) requirements for burner management systems have become more complex. The PLC (programmable logic controller) has become the logical choice to manage these systems. However, the use of PLCs for such control requires careful selection, installation, commissioning, and start-up. These conclusions are derived from experience with such systems at Weyerhaeuser Paper Company's mill in Springfield, OR. This experience is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of computer controls and display to roll grinders
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is shown that software coupled with proven hardware provides the solution for controlling the grinding variables for roll grinders. The control system presented provides the user with the following benefits: (1) the ability to grind rolls with precise motion control to obtain predictable accuracy and surface finish with a minimum of operator input; (2) computer control of the four main grinding variables, i.e. wheel speed, infeed, roll speed, and traverse; (3) reduction of machine downtime by the computer-based control interface that monitors critical operations and provides diagnostics for troubleshooting; and (4) optional on-machine caliper with display of measured roll data that enables the operator to make online corrections of the roll profiles (printout of final grind profile to specified tolerance).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Diagnostics: What is available?
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The historical progression of diagnostic systems, for electrical equipment is reviewed. An example of modern techniques is then discussed which incorporates PLCs (programmable logic controllers) and PCs in the diagnostic process. Commercially available products using these techniques are discussed. In addition, future trends are considered for the next generation of diagnostics.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cause and analysis of stator and rotor failures in 3-phase squirrel cage induction motors
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The authors attempt to identify the various causes of stator and rotor failures in three-phase squirrel cage induction motors. A specific methodology is proposed to facilitate an accurate analysis of these failures. It is noted that, due to the destructive nature of most failures, it is not easy, and is sometimes impossible, to determine the primary cause of failure. By a process of elimination, one can usually be assured of properly identifying the most likely cause of the failure. It is pointed out that the key point in going through this process of elimination is to use the basic steps of analyzing the failure class and pattern, noting the general motor appearance, identifying the operating condition at the time of failure, and gaining knowledge of the past history of the motor and application.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Capacitor application considerations-Utility/user interface
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The continuously increasing use of power capacitors throughout utility and industrial paper systems has resulted in an increased awareness level of the application considerations associated with capacitor switching and harmonics. The author reviews these topics from a system point of view, emphasizing the system interaction effects and the means that can be used to minimize this interaction. It is noted that the switching of a capacitor bank can cause transient overvoltage concerns at other points in the system under certain conditions. A number of methods are discussed for reducing these transients, including closing and opening resistors, controlled closing, staggered closing, reactors, and surge arresters. Capacitor banks throughout the system can influence the distortion level that occurs due to a harmonic source. That effect can be minimized by using filter capacitor banks in the plant at the medium or low voltage buses which would be at or near the source of the harmonics.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: DC motor and generator troubleshooting and maintenance
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Maintenance and troubleshooting tips and guidelines for motors and generators are outlined. This information is applicable to any rotating equipment except where the manufacturer is noted for specific details. In particular, it is recommended that commutation adjustment be supervised by someone who understands the theory of DC machine adjustment, is experienced in adjusting such machines, and understands the hazards involved in working with live electrical apparatus.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Shunt capacitor filters for motor starting load voltage and harmonic distortion control
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: Multipurpose shunt capacitor filters in a pulp and paper mill environment to reduce the starting voltage drop of a 23000 hp synchronous motor, provide load voltage control, and limit the harmonic current and voltage distortions in the distribution system are described. These three objectives are met by two single-tuned shunt filter banks of 10.75 and 4.6 MVAr installed on a single 13.8 kV bus. A digital computer-based study leading to the optimum design of the shunt filter banks is emphasized.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Solid cast transformers
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author provides an overview of the available types of solid cast transformers and compares the advantages and disadvantages of solid cast transformers with those of alternatives. Specifically, a comparison between different solid cast construction techniques is made in the following areas: available techniques; high voltage coils; low voltage coils; and mechanical, electrical, thermal strength, and flame test results. Also, comparisons are made between solid cast transformers and other dry-type and liquid-filled transformers. It is concluded that solid cast transformers do not present potential environmental problems, have proven to be self-extinguishing in flammability tests, can match the basic insulation levels (BILs) of liquid-filled transformers, have higher short-circuit strength, require very little maintenance, and have a very competitive total installed cost.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Characteristics and applications of various arc interrupting methods
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: It is shown that the choice of an arc interrupting means will depend upon a number of factors of the equipment involved, including cost, maintenance, reliability, space requirements, and interrupting requirements. For medium voltage applications, the above considerations and the improvement in interrupting technology and manufacturing techniques have made vacuum the dominant industry choice for 5-15 kV switchgear. Due to the third generation SF/sub 6/ puffer technology, SF/sub 6/ gas is the dominant choice for breakers above 15 kV, with some overlap with vacuum in the 15-38 kV range. For certain applications where the investment of circuit breakers is not deemed appropriate, fuses can be a viable option, with current-limiting types being the logical choice where high level fault current is available (38 kV and below). Low-voltage applications using conventional design or current limiting breaker designs are now readily available using air as the arc interrupting medium.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Safety considerations for the application, installation, operation and maintenance of industrial AC induction motors
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author identifies hazardous conditions that can cause serious damage to equipment and create unsafe conditions for personnel. The scope of the work is limited to industrial AC induction motors, even though much of it is appropriate to other types of electric motors. The hazards in terms of the potential safety. problems to exposed personnel are as follows: (1) bodily injury due to excessive temperature, fire, or explosion caused by the stator, rotor, or bearing failures; (2) electrical shock due to a dielectric breakdown or contact with live parts; (3) injury from contact with rotating members or flying parts; (4) loss of hearing from prolonged exposure to excessive noise levels; and (5) injury due to improper lifting or handling.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control systems software development survival kit
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author describes his role in a project involving the retrofit of a paper management system (PMS) Intended to provide flexibility for new products. His portion of the project was to provide the programming to replace the programmable logic controller on the 1980 vintage roll finishing line with a newer A-B PLC-5 processor to interface with a new PMS as well as to add a bar code laser scanner, sonar roll measuring scanners, a new scale, a label applicator, and a bilge stenciler. He discusses what was learned during this project and how this can be generalized to the management of control systems software development. He first gives some background information on the scope of the project undertaken. Second, he gives his opinion on how this can be extrapolated to the control of any software-based control project. Finally, he reviews the benefits of the work done on the roll finishing line project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Energy efficient lighting and lighting practices for the pulp and paper industry
publicationTitle: Conference Record of 1991 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference
abstract: The author reviews energy efficient lighting technologies, with emphasis on: the advantages and disadvantages of new lighting products; how to cope with the disadvantages; their performance and design; and how to apply these new products in an effective retrofit or in new construction applications. Current recommended lighting practices for indoor and outdoor applications are surveyed, and guidelines are established for improved techniques and economics with recommended illuminance values as applied to new projects or in the modernization of existing pulp and paper facilities.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
